text.p: Base metal prices climbed away from earlier lows during Monday afternoon LME trading, although activity remained low-key and movements took place in thin conditions.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index ended 1.95 points higher at 244.66.
Traders said copper staged a mini-rally and regained an important chart level, aluminium staved off a more precipitous decline, while nickel and zinc bounced impressively.
However, the turnaround from soggy midsession levels, which followed routine "third Wednesday" pricing, lacked conviction.
Copper pushed away from under $2,250, but still closed $15 easier at $2,257 a tonne, with further pressure expected. The cash/threes backwardation eased slightly into $35/40.
Aluminium shaved its losses as well, but still closed well below the $1,560 level it broke down through earlier.
Having fallen convincingly from near $1,600 in recent sessions, the market is set to test $1,535. Last kerb trade was at $1,549, down $15.
Zinc managed a strong rally from levels near $1,230, with the market having become oversold, and prices snapped up to close at $1,253, up $21.
Nickel prices also reversed direction during the afternoon, having staged a successful defence of the $7,100 level, and the market ended at $7,240, down just $10 from Friday.
Lead prices continued to correct upwards from Friday's 18-month lows, and although movements were fairly small. Last business was at $632, up just $5.
Tin was aided by copper's partial rally, as well as oversold technicals, and prices built on earlier modest advances, closing at $5,750, up $130.
The quiet alloy market was steady at $1,450/55 a tonne.

New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower again Monday, although volume was light and the lack of follow through to Friday's selling suggested there may not be much more downside left in the move, traders said. COMEX June gold ended down $0.60 at $348.70 an ounce after trading from $349.80 to $348.50. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted at $346.00/50 compared to the London afternoon fix of $346.75 and the New York close Friday around $346.60/$347.10.

Severe damage expected from a weekend freeze in portions of the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter belt boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to limit gains as well as a fresh seven-month high in the nearby May contract, traders said. May set a session high of $4.23 a bushel, the highest for that contract since $4.23-1/2 was notched September 11. A nine-month high was set in active new crop July of $4.28-1/4, the highest level since $4.29 was reached on July 15. September settled limit up and at its new contract high of $4.32. A buying pool of roughly 14 million bushels was noted at the close, with 10 million wanted in the July. Action in options indicated Tuesday's open for the July would be at $4.36 to $4.38 per bushel, up eight to 10 cents. Wheat closed 10-1/2 to 20 cents per bushel higher, with May up 20 at $4.23.

NYMEX oil prices ended with healthy gains Monday on a report linking Iran, the third largest oil exporter in the world, to the 1996 bombing of U.S. barracks in Saudi Arabia. The report comes at time when diplomatic tensions are already high between the West and Iran. May crude ended up 37 cents at $19.90 a barrel. Spot crude rose to a session high of $20.01, the first time spot crude rose above $20.00 since April 2. May gasoline settled 1.08 cents higher at 61.96 cents a gallon while May heating oil ended up 0.80 cent at 54.67 cents gallon.
